**Sūrat al-Jinn**, also called "Qul Ūḥiya" (Say: It has been revealed).

Its purpose is to demonstrate the nobility of this Noble Prophet, the Opener (ﷺ), and of his companions and his descendants, the people of his household. God softened the hearts of humankind, the jinn, and others toward him, so that he came to possess the hearts of his own kind and of others. This was due to the greatness of this Qur'an and the subtlety of its extraordinary status. Moreover, the time of this revelation was at its end, and the period of his stay among his people was less than a quarter of a tenth of the time of Noah (peace be upon him), the first prophet whom God sent to those who opposed Him, and only a few of his people believed with him. The name of the sūra, "al-Jinn," and the phrase "Qul Ūḥiya," indicate this. By reflecting on the verse that contains this and the subtle paths it contains, may God protect us by His grace and generosity from falling into ruin.

﴿In the name of God﴾, that is, the One encompassing all perfection, who sent His Messenger, the Seal, with guidance, that he might make it prevail over all religion by what He possesses of majesty and beauty. ﴿The Most Merciful﴾, who by the generality of His mercy embraced all this sending, so that by clarification he might cover what binds creation in speech and action. ﴿The Most Compassionate﴾, who singled out for the goodness of deeds whomever He willed among those whom he (the Messenger) distinguished as the people of the call, because of the success that had preceded for them from the beginningless beginnings.

* *

Since Noah (peace and blessings be upon him) was the first messenger God sent to those who opposed Him among the people of the earth, and his people were worshippers of idols and disobeyed him most severely, even though they were of his own lineage and language, and his sūra ends with his supplication against them, and since our Prophet (ﷺ) was the Seal of the Prophets, he is the last messenger God sent to the people of the earth and others, to all of creation. His people, the Arabs, had agreed with the people of Noah (peace be upon him) in most of their conditions, in the worship of idols, even those idols either by their names or by their forms, as is reported in the traditions. In their disobedience toward their messenger, in their oppression of his followers, and in their mockery, [the parallel] began. Here, [the mention of] the ease with which whoever heard this final, comprehensive call from outside the human kind responded, let alone those who agreed with them in kind, despite the brevity of time and the weakness of helpers, is due to the sublimity of this Qur'an. So [God] said, alerting him to this matter and to the great worth it contains, while also pointing to a reproach of the Arabs for their slowness in answering what they recognized of its rectitude in its meaning and its composition, since it was in their tongue, and since they were of the same kind as the caller, of his tribe, and closest of people to him: ﴿Say﴾, that is, O Muhammad, to your people.

Since the intended purpose is to magnify what was revealed, and the one who revealed it to each of the two messengers is one, [the verb] was put in the passive form, saying, clarifying the course of the jinn in receiving this Qur'an by taking it as an inheritance from the most noble of the prophets, and by conveying it, in delivery, to others among those who inherit knowledge from them. Thus they would have two honours: the honour of knowledge for the perfection of their own souls, and of teaching for the perfecting of others. Hence they would have a reward like that of whoever acted upon what they conveyed and dictated to him. ﴿It has been revealed to me﴾, that is, I have been informed, in a hidden manner, by the One besides whom none knows the unseen, in this Qur'an, whose inimitability required that I be the prophet most followed, through the tongue of Gabriel (peace be upon him), who is His trustworthy one and the intermediary between Him and His prophets. Then, in place of the object whose agent is not named, he put: ﴿that﴾, that is, the great matter, ﴿they listened﴾, that is, with utmost attentiveness, receptiveness, acceptance, and familiarity, a listening that is truly listening, because it was to my recitation of this Qur'an. ﴿A company﴾, who by nature and disposition are in the utmost aversion, ﴿of the jinn﴾, who are in the utmost concealment. They are living, rational bodies, light, in which the fiery or airy element predominates, just as the earthly element predominates in human bodies. A nafar (company) is between three and ten. Al-Baghawi said: they were nine, from the jinn of Nasibin; it was also said they were seven. In this expression is evidence that he (ﷺ) did not see them, nor did he recite to them; rather, their presence happened to coincide with his recitation. As for whether this listening is the one mentioned in al-Ahqaf or another, Abu Hayyan said: the well-known view is that it is that one; it was also said it is another. The jinn who came to him in Mecca were the jinn of Nasibin, and those who came to him at Nakhla were the jinn of Nineveh. The sūra they listened to, Ikrimah said, was al-'Alaq; it was also said al-Rahman. Neither here nor in al-Ahqaf does it mention that he saw them. It is evident from the traditions that the event occurred more than once. Among them is what happened at the beginning, when none of the companions, may God be pleased with them, was with him, as in the hadith of Abdullah ibn Mas'ud (may God be pleased with him), which is in the Sahih:

"They lost him (ﷺ) one night," from among the nights, "so they searched for him in the valleys and the ravines. When he rose in the morning, he came from the direction of Hira and said: 'The caller of the jinn came to me, so I went with him and recited the Qur'an to them.' Then he set off with us and showed us their traces and the traces of their fires."

Among them is what happened when Abdullah (may God be pleased with him) was with him. He went with him to al-Hajun, at the ravine, and drew a line for him and said: "Do not cross it." Then there descended upon him things like locusts, dragging stones with their feet, until they covered him, and I could not see him. He gestured to me with his hand to sit down, and he recited the Qur'an. His voice kept rising, and they disappeared into the earth, until I could no longer see them.

Al-Asbahani said: it was said they were of the Banu al-Shisban, who are the most numerous of the jinn and the main soldiers of Iblis. Al-Qushayri said: when the devils were pelted with meteors, Iblis, aware of this, sent his troops out. Seven of them came to the valley of Nakhla and listened to the recitation of the Prophet (ﷺ), and they believed. Then they went to their people and said: "O our people, we have heard a wondrous Qur'an," meaning that they did not return to Iblis, because they knew his lying and foolishness. They came to the Prophet (ﷺ) with seventy of their people, and they embraced Islam. This is the meaning of His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And when We turned toward you a company of the jinn, listening to the Qur'an; and when they attended it...﴾ [al-Ahqaf: 29], and the verses that follow. ﴿They said﴾, that is, as a consequence of their listening, one of them said to whoever had not heard, or to whoever among mankind was their companion, in compliance with the words of the Prophet (ﷺ): "May God have mercy on a man who heard a saying from us, remembered it, and conveyed it as he heard it." Their words were a calm acceptance of this Qur'an and its sources, emphasizing, because of their distance from hearing revelation and their knowledge of the inimitability it contained: ﴿Indeed, we﴾, with a kasra because it is a subject after the saying, ﴿have heard﴾, when we deliberately gave ear and directed our understanding to it, ﴿a Qur'an﴾, that is, speech that is in utmost coherence in itself and comprehensive of all that we need. Then they described it with a verbal noun for emphasis regarding its matter, saying: ﴿wondrous﴾, that is, unprecedented, outside the custom of its like among all the divine books, let alone human speech, in the majesty of its arrangement, the inimitability of its composition and construction, together with its agreement with them in calling to God, the most High, in clarifying goodness and evil, and in calling to every success, until it became the very embodiment of wonder. A wonder is what goes beyond the limits of its kinds and counterparts, so its cause is hidden. This indicates their scholarly strength in eloquence, and their perfection in the science of forms and the shaping of speech in the most eloquent manner of arrangement.

Abu Ja'far ibn al-Zubayr said: Since the condition of the disbelievers of Quraysh had been mentioned earlier, in their turning away from reflection and their persistence in obstinacy and stubbornness, as contained in Sūrat Nun wal-Qalam; then it was followed by their threat in al-Haqqa; then by its confirmation and nearness of occurrence in al-Ma'arij; then by consoling him, peace be upon him, and comforting him with the story of Noah (peace be upon him) and his people, He followed that with what the one granted success takes heed of, and knows that hearts are in the hand of God. The response of the stubborn ones of Quraysh and the Arabs was, in outward appearance, nearer to a prophet of their own kind and of themselves, for his truthfulness and trustworthiness had already been known to them. Then he came to them with a Book in the tongue by which they converse, and in the language by which they speak. His signs dazzled the intellects, and his proofs and miracles became clear to everyone with a sound heart. They knew they could not produce its equal, given the great proofs they had witnessed. Yet despite this, they were blind and deaf, may God be angry with them and curse them. And there preceded to faith one who was not of their kind and did not have the distinction of their honour, namely the jinn, of those for whom the good had already been decreed by God. They believed and affirmed. The Prophet (ﷺ) was commanded to report this, so God sent down to him: ﴿Say: It has been revealed to me that a company of the jinn listened...﴾ up to His saying, giving information about the jinn informing their brethren about what they had witnessed of the obstinacy of the disbelieving Arabs. And [it is reported] that when Abdullah stood calling him, they nearly became a mass upon him (ləbadan). Then the verses continued, interlocking in meaning and reinforcing in structure, to the end of the sūra. End quote.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 72, verse 2:

When they had explained its excellence in respect of its inimitability (i'jaz) and other aspects, they then explained the principal purpose, which indicates that they had plunged into its meanings after knowing the excellence of its expressions. They said: ﴿It guides﴾, that is, it makes clear the utmost clarity, together with the call, in gentleness and guidance, ﴿to right conduct (al-rushd)﴾, that is, the truth and the correct course, which nearly slips away because of its heaviness upon souls that are inclined to desire and lightness, whose opposite is error (al-ghayy) and foolishness (al-safah), which suits the deficiencies of souls. When they had described it with these perfections, they stated as a consequence of that their saying, employing the practical faculty in hastening to what is correct without any hesitation at all: ﴿So we believed in it﴾, that is, everyone among us who listened did not hold back, and not one of us lagged behind or hesitated after listening, ﴿in it﴾, that is, we gave security to the one who conveys the Qur'an that we would not deny it or oppose it in the slightest opposition because of this Qur'an.

When they reported about the past, and since faith is only beneficial when it continues, (p-467) they said, joining it by conjunction to what is implied in the sense of: "So we found God in the present," because that is the result of belief in the Qur'an and our renouncing of rivals: ﴿And we will never﴾, that is, while we are in the state of having brought faith into effect now, we will never at all, after that, ﴿associate﴾ [anyone]. They emphasized it because it is a matter that hardly seems credible, ﴿with our Lord﴾, that is, the One upon Whom no benefaction resting on us, from bringing into existence and what follows it, is except from Him, ﴿anyone﴾, that is, of creation, because no one shares with Him in any of our affairs. The proofs of monotheism have been made clear in what we heard of this Qur'an.

When they had demonstrated their intellectual capacity, through their understanding of the Qur'an, and their practical capacity, through the submission that had taken hold of them, they put to use the eloquence they possessed in calling to God, the Exalted. So, after they had declared Him far above association (shirk) in general, they specified, with emphasis, in the recitation of Ibn Kathir, the Basrans, and Abu Ja'far, using the kasra (in *wa-annahu*), because of what preceded: that such ease is hardly believable. They said, by coordination ('atf) upon ﴿Indeed, we have heard﴾ [al-Jinn: 1], ﴿and that He﴾, that is, the great matter. The jinn said: ﴿Exalted is the majesty of our Lord﴾, that is, He has reached such a height of elevation and loftiness that it cannot be attained. ﴿Majesty﴾ means greatness, sovereignty, and perfect self-sufficiency. ﴿Our Lord﴾, that is, the One who brought us into existence and who is good to us. If this exaltedness belongs to His majesty, then consider what He Himself is.

Likewise, this recitation relates, through the jinn's words, everything that follows this, namely ﴿and that if they had remained upright﴾ [al-Jinn: 16], ﴿and that the mosques are for God﴾ [al-Jinn: 18], and ﴿and that when the servant of God stood up﴾ [al-Jinn: 19]. In these, it is read with a fatha, by coordination upon "what has been revealed" (al-muhan bihi), so it is in the position of a nominative (raf'). The exception is Abu Ja'far, who read with a fatha ﴿and that He, exalted be He﴾, and ﴿and that he used to say﴾ [al-Jinn: 4], and ﴿and that there were men﴾ [al-Jinn: 6]. Nafi' and Abu Bakr, on the authority of 'Asim, agreed with them, except in ﴿and that when he stood up﴾ [al-Jinn: 19], where both read with a kasra. The rest read with a fatha: Ibn 'Amir, Hamzah, al-Kisa'i, and Hafs on the authority of 'Asim, in all cases except those introduced by the particle fa'. This is by coordination upon the position of the prepositional phrase in "bihi" (in Him), that is, "we believed in Him and we believed that He..." It is not coordination upon its wording, since otherwise the repetition of the preposition would be required according to the grammarians of Basra. It was also said that it is coordinated upon the wording of the pronoun in "bihi," according to the Kufan school, which was upheld by Abu Hayyan and many other masters of the language.

When they described Him with this supreme exaltedness, which entails absolute self-sufficiency and freedom from every trace of deficiency, they clarified it by negating what contradicts it, saying, nullifying falsehood: ﴿He has not taken﴾. The form *ittakhadha* (the reflexive pattern) is used to indicate the locus of deficiency, not as a restriction. ﴿a consort﴾, that is, a wife. ﴿nor a son﴾, because the custom is that this occurs only through treatment and causation, and such things occur only for one who is in need of a mate or something else. Need arises only from weakness and incapacity, and that contradicts majesty. So the one who is in need cannot at all be a god, even if it occurs without causation or delay, since this would be pointless, for mere origination suffices without it. Nothing remains but the futility from which God is exempt. A consort must be of the same kind as her spouse, and whoever has a kind is composed of a common attribute and a distinguishing attribute, rationally composed. A son must be a part separated from his father, and whoever has parts is composed in a sensible (physical) composition. It is certain that this occurs only for one who is in need, and that God, the Exalted, is far above this, whether a sensible or a rational composition.

"When it became clear to them how far He, glory be to Him, is above every trace of deficiency, they described as foolish the one who had said the opposite, safeguarding their religion and their honour by rising above base and vile things, by not persisting in falsehood out of abhorrence of creatures for the sake of the creature, emphasising what a listener generally has of believing what he hears and of disputing about it. So they said: ﴿And that﴾, i.e., and they said, 'Indeed the matter is...' — this is according to the reading with kasra — and 'We believed that' — according to the reading with fatha — ﴿he, our foolish one, used to say﴾, i.e., a saying which, in its deep-rootedness in falsehood, is like innate nature and disposition, ﴿foolish﴾ (safih), which is a generic term, so it includes Iblis, the head of the jinn, in the first place, and everyone who followed him among those who did not know Allah, because the fruit of intellect is knowledge, and the fruit of knowledge is knowing Allah; so whoever does not know Him is the one who is constantly attached to recklessness and error, since he has no knowledge at all to restrain him toward sound judgement, lying and fabricating ﴿against Allah﴾ (p-470), i.e., the One who possesses the attributes of perfection which contradict the claim of this fool concerning offspring, ﴿an outrageous transgression﴾, i.e., a saying which in its remoteness from the right is itself remoteness, and exceeding the bounds."

When they had mentioned what they had been guided to of the truth concerning God, and concerning the one who used to lead them into falsehood, they mentioned their excuse for following the fool and for falling into places of suspicion. They said, emphasizing (because what they had been upon of disbelief was worthy of being thought not to be hidden from anyone, due to the great clarity of its falsehood): ﴿And we﴾, that is, we company of Muslims among the jinn, ﴿thought﴾, that is, by what we possessed of soundness of natural disposition, which requires thinking well (of others), as attested by the hadith of Abu Hurayrah, may Allah be pleased with him, in Ahmad: "The believer is gullible and generous, and the wicked is deceptive and base." ﴿that﴾, that is, that it (i.e., humankind and jinn) ﴿would never say﴾. They increased the emphasis regarding what had passed, saying: ﴿would never say﴾, and they began with the better of the two kinds, saying: ﴿the humans﴾, and they followed them with their companions, saying: ﴿and the jinn﴾, that is, fabricating ﴿against Allah﴾, that is, the Sovereign Above, in whose hand is benefit and harm, ﴿a lie﴾, that is, a statement which, by its ancient persistence in opposing reality, is itself the very essence of lying. In the reading of Abu Ja'far, it is with a fatha on the qaf and a fatha on the shadda-ed waw, which is a verbal noun (masdar) not derived from the verb's own form (min ghayr al-lafz). We thought this only because of what the one created to desire the passions is disposed to, namely the acceptance of similar things, especially when their statement is firm and grave, such as is not said except after careful verification, especially when it concerns the King of kings, especially when the speaker is many, especially when they are reinforced by another kind, so that they become innumerable in multitude, and the intellects cannot withstand opposing a group with this description except by a divine support with a textual decisive proof. The verse, in Abu Ja'far's reading, is of the device of ihtibak (interlocking): the verb of fabricating (taqawwul) first indicates the act of lying second, and the noun of lying second indicates the noun of fabricating first. Its secret is that taqawwul indicates deliberateness, so it is more vile in meaning, while kadhib is more vile in wording. This guides to the conclusion that one should not follow blind imitation (taqlid) in anything, because trust in every person is incapacity, and it is only revealed through testing; and blind imitation may lead to disbelief that destroys, an everlasting destruction. To this the Prophet ﷺ also guided, in what al-Shaykhan (al-Bukhari and Muslim) narrated from al-Nu'man ibn Bashir, may Allah be pleased with him, that "whoever avoids doubtful matters has cleared his religion and his honour." And in this is the utmost exhortation that a person should neither advance nor hold back in the foundations of the religion except with a decisive proof.

When al-Biqa'i realised from their words that the basis of error is conjecture and dubious claims, which fall apart once they are rubbed against the touchstone of reflection, and whose falsity the assayers expose, he followed it with another doubt. It increased both groups in error, each through the other, because they were bound to sensory things and stopped at imagined fancies. So he said, quoting them, as a warning against being deceived by praise and flattery, which lead to error in the soul, and to the point that one must be careful, so that no mistake is made about the subordinate causes, and one does not think they are effective, thereby going beyond their rank of contingent things to the rank of the Necessary Being. He stressed this because it is hardly believable that jinn would address humans and show them honour: ﴿And that﴾, i.e., the matter, ﴿there were men﴾, i.e., people of strength and might, ﴿from among mankind﴾, i.e., the apparent species in the world of the human kind, ﴿who used to seek refuge﴾, i.e., they would take shelter and seek protection, out of fear for themselves and what they had with them, ﴿in men of the jinn﴾ when they halted in a valley, i.e., the tribe hidden from sight. For when a group of them alighted in a valley or another barren place, the jinn would sometimes toy with them, since there was nothing to restrain them, as they had no remembrance of God Most High, no sound religion, and no clear Book from God. This led them to seek the protection of the jinn's great ones. A man would say, when afraid: "I seek refuge with the great one of this valley from the evil of the foolish ones of his people," or something similar, and he would see nothing but good. Often they would guide him to the road and return his lost property to him. This was a trial for mankind, since they believed in the jinn what was not true of them, and so they followed them into error. The trial of the jinn was that they would become proud of themselves and say, "Our lord is among the jinn and mankind," and thus they would go astray and lead others astray. Therefore he linked to this his saying: ﴿so they increased them﴾, i.e., mankind increased the jinn, through this seeking of refuge, which was followed by their being given protection, and the jinn increased mankind, by making them leaders over them and by their fear of them, ﴿in burden﴾, i.e., in distress, hardship and overwhelming, because of the states of error they were in, which necessarily bring constriction and hardship. The root of rahaq is overwhelming with force, might and domination. Al-Baghawi said: "In the language of the Arabs, rahaq means sin and the violation of what is forbidden."

This is like what happens to one of the people of tasawwuf (Sufism, the mystical path) who travels without a proper foundation. In the course of his journey he sees lights and things that please him, which are satanic, but he thinks they are from the Merciful. He halts at them and takes comfort in them, because of corruption in his innate nature, which results in the badness of his intention. Often this becomes the cause of his disbelief, and so he and those like him among mankind increase in error, and those among the jinn who misled him increase in error and in [misleading and] arrogance. The two groups grow further from turning to God alone. God, glorified and exalted, has made us independent of everything through the Qur'an and the remembrance taken from the best of His creation, under its conditions and at its appointed times, as the Prophet (ﷺ) informed us: whoever says upon entering the toilet, "In the name of God. O God, I seek refuge in You from the male and female unclean spirits," is shielded from the jinn. And whoever says when he approaches his wife, "O God, keep Satan away from us, and keep Satan away from what You grant us," and a child is born to them, Satan will not be able to harm him. Whoever does this is secure from being seized by ghouls. And al-Tirmidhi and Ahmad narrated, on the authority of Shaddad ibn Aws (may God be pleased with him), that the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "No Muslim lies down on his bed and recites a surah from the Book of God, the Exalted, except that God appoints an angel over him, and nothing that harms him will come near him until he wakes up, whenever he wakes." (al-Mundhiri said: its narrators are those of the Sahih.) And al-Tabarani in al-Kabir narrated, on the authority of Abdullah ibn Bisr (may God be pleased with him), who said: "I left Homs, and the night overtook me at al-Buqay'a. Some of the inhabitants of the earth came upon me, so I recited this verse from al-A'raf:

﴿Indeed, your Lord is God, who created the heavens and the earth in six days, then established Himself upon the Throne﴾ [al-A'raf: 54], to the end of the verse. Then some of them said to others: 'Guard him now until morning.' When I awoke, I mounted my mount." (Al-Mundhiri said: its narrators are those of the Sahih, except al-Musayyab ibn Wadih. Al-Haythami said: he is weak, but he is considered reliable.)

The narrations on this are numerous, concerning Ayat al-Kursi and other verses, and likewise the accounts of those whom some jinn confronted, and when they recited, the jinn departed from them.
